title: Influences on the Uptake of and Engagement With Health and Well-Being Smartphone Apps: Systematic Review
extended_summary:
This systematic review examines what influences adults to download, adopt, and continue using health and well-being smartphone apps. The paper was motivated by the observation that digital health interventions often have limited public health impact because uptake is low and engagement declines quickly, even when apps are designed to support behavior change.

The review synthesized evidence from 41 quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods studies published between 2011 and 2019. It focused on smartphone apps related to smoking cessation, alcohol reduction, physical activity, diet, mental health, and broader health/well-being, and mapped the identified factors onto the COM-B model and Theoretical Domains Framework. The studies included a range of adult populations, such as the general public, existing app users, patients in primary care, college students, and several condition-specific or community groups.

The review concludes that uptake and engagement are shaped by a broad set of factors, including app literacy, awareness, guidance, credible health information, reminders, low cognitive burden, self-monitoring, low cost, personalization, recommendations from trusted sources, practitioner support, social networking, positive feedback, rewards, goal setting, and perceived utility. Overall, the authors argue that improving app design, tailoring content, and supporting social and professional connections may strengthen real-world use of health apps.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review, but it does not evaluate an AI tool or report AI-specific outcomes. The paper synthesizes qualitative and quantitative evidence about smartphone app uptake/engagement factors.
impact_tier_rationale: No AI intervention effect is reported, so there is no measurable impact tier to assign for generative AI or any other AI tool.
